cells.tense: You are sitting at the bench right now, pen in hand, and the proportions are coming right.
cells.act: refine one distinction by close attention
cells.ask: Find one small distinction in what you make — the knot that holds against the knot that gives — and give it your whole attention once. Name it when you finish, then leave the rest of the work where it sits.
cells.core:
When you're at the bench, the work gets finer by itself. Each pass shows you something the last one couldn't, and you don't force it — the practice has a current and you're in it. Being alone with it connects you instead of closing you off, and you come back more useful than you left.

What keeps it clean is that you're sharpening the eye, not the worry. So today, take one small distinction — the cut that holds against the cut that gives — and give it your attention once, then name it plainly. The rest stays where it is. One pass, and stop. That's the whole ask, and it's how refinement stays a pleasure instead of a debt.
cells.sheetLine: One pass, and the eye gets sharper.

cells.tense: You are bracing at a bench that hasn't been built yet, and the proportions already feel wrong.
cells.act: let the gladness go out to the room
cells.ask: Let the good thing that's already here reach whoever is near you — say it while it's fresh, not in a report tomorrow. One piece of it, shared now, before you move on.
cells.core:
The work is being planned past where the work can go. Every stage is checked against a version of it that doesn't exist yet, and the checking is outrunning the making. What got built to keep the craft honest is now measuring it against a future nobody can write in. Whoever is close to you is getting the corrections, not the thing that went well.

So let one real piece of it reach them — the part that already holds — while it's still warm. Saying the good thing out loud is not a reward after the work; it's part of the work, and it's how the practice stays something you're in rather than something you're behind. One good thing, said now, before you move on.

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door that's already behind you, waiting to be let in.
cells.act: put the frame on the table before anyone asks
cells.ask: Say what you're building and where it actually stands — plainly, once, out loud, to whoever is nearest. No prefacing it, no shrinking it. Let the sentence be enough, and stop there.
cells.core:
The bench sits empty while you measure yourself against what the work should be by now, and the measuring keeps you outside. Nothing here gets claimed until it's said aloud, and yours keeps going unsaid. That is why it doesn't feel like the thing is yours to own.

So set what you're making on the table in plain words, unpolished, no apology first. That is how the door stops being a door. One plain statement and the ground under you is real again, and you can pick the work back up from there. Say it once, and leave it said.

cells.tense: The pen is down in a room where you are already writing the thing.
cells.act: move at the pace your feeling can sustain
cells.ask: Work at the speed your own wanting sets, and keep it steady — this is a hold, not a burst. Let it run one stretch, then stop and notice what carried.
cells.core:
The craft is yours and you describe it as if it happened to you. You talk about the practice like it comes and goes, while your hand is what's on the pen. The ones who benefit from it have no way to tell you otherwise, because the telling isn't in their view.

Before it was this deep, it was just something you liked. Go back there for one stretch. Work at the speed your own wanting sets, not the speed the outcome demands, and keep going at that pace past the point where a burst would have quit. Not a break, not a surge. That first pace was yours; the craft sits on it, not the other way around.
